front: Per the abstract, what does a threads facility give a program and how do the threads coordinate?
back: Multiple simultaneous points of execution that synchronize through shared memory.

front: Who is the paper aimed at, per the abstract?
back: Experienced programmers wanting practical expertise; it describes each primitive then gives a tutorial per primitive with advice, warnings about what goes wrong, and hints for avoiding pitfalls.

front: How is the body of the paper structured?
back: One tutorial section per primitive (Mutex, Condition variable, Fork, Alert), then additional techniques, building programs, and an appendix comparing other thread designs.

front: At the time of writing, what was the most popular concurrency mechanism in operating systems?
back: Multiple lightweight threads within a single address space, used from within a single program.

front: Why does Birrell call deadlock "a pleasant sort of bug"?
back: The program stops with all the evidence intact; other pitfalls instead take the form of insidious performance penalties.

front: What is the paper's stated goal?
back: To give an experienced sequential programmer enough hints to build a substantial multi-threaded program that works correctly, efficiently, and with a minimum of surprises.

text: Birrell defines a thread as {{c1::a single sequential flow of control}}; within one thread there is a single point of execution at any instant.
extra: In a high-level language a thread is programmed with procedures whose calls follow the traditional stack discipline, and the programmer needs to learn nothing new to use a single thread.

front: With multiple threads, what mostly-true view can the programmer take, and what must they occasionally remember?
back: They can mostly view the threads as executing simultaneously, as if there were as many processors as threads, but must occasionally remember that they might not all actually run simultaneously.

front: What does "single address space" mean for threads, per Birrell?
back: The addressing hardware is configured so all threads can read and write the same memory locations; off-stack (global) variables are shared, while each thread runs on its own call stack with its own local variables.

text: Birrell's definition of {{c1::lightweight}}: thread creation, existence, destruction and synchronization are cheap enough that the programmer will use them for all concurrency needs.

front: How does Birrell use the word "process" (footnote 1)?
back: Only for a single flow of control associated one-to-one with an address space, since that seemed the most common usage.

front: Birrell describes the paper as selective, biased, and idiosyncratic. What does each mean?
back: Selective: only the most important primitives, omitting features such as per-thread context. Biased: built around the design choices of the Topaz system at SRC. Idiosyncratic: based on the author's ten years of personal experience.

front: In what language are the paper's examples written, and how should they be treated?
back: Modula-2+ (Algol/Pascal family); they illustrate concurrency points only and should not be used as algorithms in real programs.

front: Are threads a tool for automatic parallel decomposition?
back: No. Automatic parallel decomposition (a compiler turning a sequential program into multiprocessor code) is a different art the paper does not cover.

front: What four forces push toward concurrency, per Birrell?
back: (1) multiprocessors; (2) driving slow devices (disks, networks, terminals, printers); (3) human users, who do two or three things at once; (4) distributed systems with shared network servers (file server, spooling print server).

front: Why is the multiprocess (separate address spaces) alternative to threads unattractive?
back: It is expensive to set up and inter-address-space communication is often costly even in the presence of shared segments.

front: On how many processors were lightweight threads observed to work well?
back: Up to about 10 processors, not 1000.

front: How are slow devices programmed with threads?
back: Every device request is treated as sequential: it suspends only the invoking thread until completion, while other threads do useful work.

front: How do window systems typically use threads?
back: Each user-invoked action (e.g. a mouse click) runs in a separate thread so multiple actions run in parallel; the window system itself probably also uses a thread to watch the mouse (another slow device).

front: Why do servers use multiple threads, per Birrell?
back: To handle client requests in parallel, instead of artificially serializing them or creating one server process per client "at great expense."

text: Birrell defines {{c1::latency}} as the elapsed time between calling a procedure and its return; concurrency can reduce it by deferring work that does not affect the result to another thread.
extra: Example: return from a balanced-tree insert/delete before re-balancing, and re-balance in a separate thread.

front: Why is deferring work to a lower-priority thread valuable even on a uniprocessor?
back: The deferred work happens when the system is less busy (e.g. waiting for user input): the same total work, but better responsiveness.

front: What are the four major mechanisms of a thread facility, and which does the lecture cover?
back: Thread creation, mutual exclusion, waiting for events, and a way to get a thread out of an unwanted long-term wait (alerts).
source: The design of a thread facility

front: Around whose thread facility is the paper organized, and where were its semantics specified?
back: The SRC thread facility; its semantics were formally specified in reference [4] (Birrell, Guttag, Horning, Levin, SOSP 1987).
source: The design of a thread facility

front: What does Fork do in the SRC interface?
back: It starts a new thread executing asynchronously at an invocation of the given procedure; when that procedure returns, the thread dies.

front: In the SRC thread interface, what is REFANY?
back: A dynamically typed pointer to garbage-collected storage (footnote 2).

front: What does t := Fork(a, x); p := b(y); q := Join(t); do?
back: Runs a(x) and b(y) in parallel and assigns a(x)'s result to q.

front: Why is Join rarely called at SRC (and absent from some facilities)?
back: Most forked threads are permanent daemon threads, have no results, or communicate results through some other synchronization arrangement.

front: How does SRC express mutual exclusion?
back: With the data type Mutex and the language construct LOCK mutex DO ... END, which locks, runs the statements, then unlocks.

front: What are the two states of a mutex and its initial state, and what happens to a second thread?
back: Locked and unlocked, initially unlocked. A thread inside the LOCK clause "holds" it; a second thread trying to lock it blocks, enqueued on the mutex, until it is unlocked.

front: Associating variables with a mutex and accessing them only while holding it is the basis of what construct, first described by whom?
back: Monitors, first described by Tony Hoare (reference [9]).

front: With a global mutex, the invariant is "at most one thread inside the LOCK clause." What is the correct statement for a mutex stored in a record?
back: "At most one thread executes with that mutex held": the mutex protects the other fields of the same record, so different records can be accessed in parallel.

front: How can a mutex be viewed as a scheduling mechanism, and why do condition variables exist?
back: A mutex is a simple resource scheduler: resource is the shared memory in the LOCK clause, policy is one thread at a time. Condition variables express more complicated scheduling policies by letting a thread block until some event happens.

front: What does a monitor consist of, per Birrell?
back: Some data, a mutex, and zero or more condition variables; a given condition variable is always used with the same mutex and its data.

front: What does Signal do when there are no waiters, and when there are?
back: With no waiter it does nothing (a signal is not remembered). If there are waiters it awakens at least one, but possibly more than one.

front: What race does the atomic unlock-and-block in Wait avoid (footnote 3)?
back: The "wake-up waiting" race.

front: What is the purpose of an Alert?
back: To interrupt a particular thread so it backs out of a long-term wait or computation.

front: What operations make up the SRC alert interface?
back: EXCEPTION Alerted, Alert(t: Thread), AlertWait(m, c), and TestAlert(): BOOLEAN. The notes only mention in passing that Birrell describes mechanisms for waking threads from a wait state.

front: What per-thread state do alerts use, and how does AlertWait behave?
back: Each thread has an "alert-pending" boolean, initially false. AlertWait behaves like Wait except that if alert-pending is true it does not block: it clears the flag, re-locks m, and raises Alerted.

front: What does Alert(t) do to a thread blocked in AlertWait versus a thread not blocked in AlertWait?
back: On a thread in AlertWait it wakes it, which re-locks the mutex and raises Alerted. On a thread not in AlertWait (including one in plain Wait) it only sets the alert-pending flag.

front: What does TestAlert do?
back: Atomically tests and clears the calling thread's alert-pending boolean.

front: How should Modula-2+ exceptions be thought of?
back: As a non-ignorable return code.

front: In the GetChar/CANCEL example, why use Alert instead of signalling the condition variable?
back: The condition variable may be hidden under layers of abstraction, so signalling it is not possible; the CANCEL thread instead calls Thread.Alert(t) and GetChar catches Alerted to return EndOfFile.

front: What does Birrell say about the complexity of alerts?
back: "Alerts are complicated, and their use produces complicated programs."

front: State Birrell's basic rule for shared data, and how its wording differs from the notes.
back: All shared mutable data must be associated with some mutex and accessed only by a thread holding it. The notes say "shared state" without the mutable qualifier; immutable data needs no lock.
source: Using a Mutex: accessing shared data

front: In the unprotected table-Insert example, what does interleaving A(1), B(1), A(2), B(2) of Insert(x) and Insert(y) produce?
back: y is left in the table, x is lost, and since step (2) ran twice there is an orphaned empty (NIL) slot. Fix: wrap steps (1) and (2) in LOCK m DO ... END.

front: Why can the effects of unsynchronized access be bizarre?
back: They depend on precise timing, which is usually non-deterministic due to page faults, real-time timer facilities, or actual multiprocessor asynchrony.

front: In 1989, what help could the language give against unprotected data, and what did Birrell say was actually available?
back: Ideally syntax preventing access to variables until the appropriate mutex is locked, but most languages did not offer this; meanwhile you need programmer discipline and careful use of searching and browsing tools.

front: What is the tradeoff of coarse-grain locking, and Birrell's advice on mutex complexity?
back: Coarse-grain locking makes unprotected-data bugs rarer but causes lock conflicts. Make mutex use "as simple as possible, but no simpler"; adopt elaborate arrangements only if benefits clearly outweigh risks, not because the program looks nicer.

front: How should you think of a mutex in terms of invariants?
back: As protecting the invariant of its data: a boolean function of the data true whenever the mutex is not held. A thread that locks it starts with the invariant true and must restore it before releasing, including before calling Wait (since Wait unlocks).

front: What is the invariant of the table example, and when is it false?
back: i is the index of the first NIL element and all elements beyond i are NIL. It is false between the two assignments and is guaranteed only when the mutex is not held.

front: What does Birrell advise about writing down invariants?
back: Write them down explicitly; if they are too complicated to write down, you are probably doing something wrong. They can be informal or in a formal specification language such as Larch [7], which was used to specify the SRC threads facility.

front: Why are programmers tempted to "cheat" and skip the mutex for simple data?
back: The mutex has significant overhead, and for a single integer or boolean they "know" the access is a single atomic instruction.

front: Under what conditions does skipping the lock probably work, and what is the risk otherwise?
back: Only if the variable is word aligned, the machine is a uniprocessor, and the compiler generates the obvious instructions and does not cache the variable in a register. Otherwise you may get wrong answers, or worse, usually right and occasionally wrong.

front: Per Birrell, what must machine-independent correct code use instead of relying on instruction atomicity?
back: A synchronization technique approved by the language.

front: What does Birrell's footnote 4 say about letting programmers exploit instruction atomicity to avoid a LOCK clause?
back: There is a strong argument for allowing it, but it is hard to define such a feature efficiently and machine-independently.

text: Birrell defines a {{c1::hint}} as a cheap way of getting information that is either correct or causes you to invoke a more expensive, correct way of getting it; unsynchronized reads can be used as hints.

front: In the double-checked initialization hint, what three assumptions must the language guarantee for it to be correct?
back: initDone starts FALSE, an unlocked read cannot cause a runtime error, and an unlocked read of FALSE returns FALSE. Reading a stale FALSE merely costs taking the lock; verify the language guarantees these before using it.

front: What is the simplest deadlock involving only mutexes, and how do some systems allow it?
back: A thread trying to lock a mutex it already holds; some systems explicitly allow the thread to continue (recursive locking; e.g. Sun).

front: How is a lock-order rule stated to avoid mutex-only deadlocks, and what does it not avoid?
back: As a partial order: for any pair {M1, M2}, every thread needing both locks them in the same order. This completely avoids deadlocks involving only mutexes, but not other deadlocks that arise with condition variables.

front: What is the partitioning technique for enabling a lock partial order?
back: If thread B wanting M1 actually needs data disjoint from what A accesses under M1, protect that disjoint data with a new mutex M3, giving order M1 before M2 before M3. It exists only to enable a partial order.

front: What does Birrell say about deadlock risk versus wrong answers?
back: "Having your program deadlock is almost always a preferable risk to having your program give the wrong answer." Pursuing partitioning makes locking more complicated and unsynchronized access more likely.

front: Once all data is protected and granularity is fine enough not to deadlock, what kind of mutex problems remain?
back: All of them are performance problems.

front: When does holding a mutex hurt throughput, and why is it worse on a multiprocessor?
back: When the holder stops progressing while holding it (blocks on another mutex, takes a page fault, waits for I/O). On a multiprocessor a blocked thread may leave a processor idle. Lock conflicts must be rare events.

front: What is the inherent dilemma of lock granularity?
back: Finer granularity reduces conflicts but adds complexity; "There is no way out of this dilemma" since it is a tradeoff inherent in concurrent computation.

front: In the open-files example, why is a single mutex for open/close/read/write bad, and what is the fix?
back: It would prevent writes to separate files proceeding in parallel. Fix: a globalLock protects the global table in Open, and each File record holds its own mutex, with Write(f, ...) doing LOCK f^.m DO ... END.

front: Can different parts of one record be protected by different mutexes? What about immutable fields?
back: Yes, different parts can be protected by different mutexes; immutable fields of a record need no protection at all.

front: What is the packed-field hazard with per-field mutexes?
back: If fields packed into one memory word (not separately accessible by atomic operations) are protected by different mutexes, concurrent read-modify-write of the whole word by two threads can corrupt the other field. Be careful when overriding the default record layout.

front: What is the scheduler, per Birrell, and how does it usually choose threads?
back: The part of the thread implementation (often in the OS) that decides which non-blocked threads get a processor, usually by priority; priorities may be fixed or dynamic, programmer-assigned or computed, and the algorithm is often unspecified.

front: Describe Birrell's scenario (uniprocessor, A high, B medium, C low) in which a high-priority thread is stuck behind lower-priority ones, now called priority inversion (Birrell does not use that name).
back: C locks M; B wakes and preempts C; B starts a very long computation; A wakes and preempts B; A tries to lock M and blocks; the processor returns to B. A cannot progress while B uses the CPU, and the state is stable until C gets CPU time to unlock M.

front: In the scenario now called priority inversion (Birrell does not name it), what programmer workaround does Birrell give, and what is its drawback?
back: C raises its priority before locking M. It is inconvenient because it requires knowing, per mutex, which other priorities might be involved.

front: In the scenario now called priority inversion (Birrell does not name it), what does Birrell say the thread implementer should do?
back: While A is blocked on M, the scheduler should treat M's holder as having at least A's priority (the technique now called priority inheritance; not Birrell's term). The SRC implementation does not do this.

front: Why might you release the mutex within a LOCK clause, and what does SRC provide for it?
back: To unlock before calling down into a lower-level abstraction that will block or run long, avoiding delaying other threads. SRC provides raw Acquire(m) and Release(m) in a lower-level, less-advertised interface.
source: Releasing the mutex within a LOCK clause

front: What are the dangers of releasing the mutex within a LOCK clause?
back: The calls must be correctly bracketed even when exceptions occur, and the monitor data may change while unlocked. If Release is inside a flow-control construct, the program counter encodes a decision based on old monitor state that may no longer be valid. SRC discourages this.
source: Releasing the mutex within a LOCK clause

front: What is mutex hand-off to a forked thread, and what is Birrell's recommendation?
back: Holding a mutex, fork a thread to continue working on the protected data (child locks with Acquire and calls Release) while the parent stops touching it. It is dangerous, hard to verify, and fails on facilities that track which thread holds a mutex. Birrell recommends against it.
source: Releasing the mutex within a LOCK clause

front: In the unbounded producer/consumer buffer, why does one condition variable suffice (contrast with the notes)?
back: Because the buffer is unbounded, producers never wait, so only consumers block (on nonEmpty); one condition variable suffices. The notes' bounded buffer needs two (c_prod and c_cons).
source: Using a Condition variable: scheduling shared resources

text: Birrell strongly recommends that all condition variable use follow the pattern {{c1::WHILE NOT expression DO Thread.Wait(m,c) END}}.
source: Using a Condition variable: scheduling shared resources

front: Per footnote 5, why does SRC not use Hoare's condition variables even though Hoare's design makes the re-test redundant?
back: SRC's design is preferred because it permits a much simpler implementation and the extra check is usually cheap. (These are the Mesa-style semantics; the paper lists Lampson and Redell's Mesa paper [10].)
source: Using a Condition variable: scheduling shared resources

front: Reason 2 (specific to SRC) for the while loop: what can Signal rarely do, and why is this allowed?
back: Signal may rarely wake more than one thread; this is permitted because it allowed more efficient code for Wait and Signal.
source: Using a Condition variable: scheduling shared resources

front: What is Birrell's main reason for the while-loop convention?
back: With the loop it is immediately clear the expression holds before the following statements; without it this could be verified only by examining every place that might signal. The convention allows verifying correctness by local inspection rather than global inspection.
source: Using a Condition variable: scheduling shared resources

front: What is the final advantage of the re-check convention regarding extra wake-ups?
back: Extra wake-ups are benign, so coding to wake only the right threads becomes a performance question rather than a correctness one (though at least the correct threads must still be woken).
source: Using a Condition variable: scheduling shared resources

front: What is the named example of a genuine need for Broadcast?
back: Shared/exclusive (readers/writers) locking: reads may proceed concurrently (correct and faster), but a modifying thread needs exclusive access. Callers bracket reads with AcquireShared/ReleaseShared and writes with AcquireExclusive/ReleaseExclusive.

front: Why is Broadcast only a convenience in ReleaseExclusive, not a necessity?
back: The terminating writer need not know how many readers can proceed, but you could instead keep a count of waiting readers and call Signal that many times. Broadcast just uses information the thread implementation already has.

front: In the one-CV readers/writers code, how does ReleaseExclusive's Broadcast cause a spurious wake-up, and what does it cost?
back: The Broadcast wakes readers and writers; if a reader locks the mutex first it increments i and the woken writer cannot progress until ReleaseShared. The cost is extra time in the thread scheduler, "typically an expensive place to be."

front: How does the refined readers/writers version reduce spurious wake-ups?
back: Split waiters onto two condition variables (cR, cW): a terminating reader signals only the writers' CV, and a terminating writer signals one of the two depending on which is non-empty (Broadcast cR if readWaiters > 0, else Signal cW).

front: What does Birrell call "spurious lock conflicts," and how do they arise?
back: A terminating reader calls Signal while still holding the mutex; on a multiprocessor the woken writer runs a few instructions in Wait and blocks on the still-held mutex, then microseconds later the reader unlocks it. Cost: two extra re-schedule operations, "a significant expense."

front: Is a spurious lock conflict usually a problem on a uniprocessor?
back: No; on a uniprocessor it is often not a problem.

front: Why is a terminating writer's Broadcast a harder case for spurious lock conflicts?
back: The Broadcast is issued with the mutex held, and only one woken reader at a time can lock the mutex to re-check and increment i, so on a multiprocessor the other woken readers tend to block on the mutex.

front: What is the chained-wake-up fix for the writer's Broadcast case?
back: ReleaseExclusive Signals one reader instead of Broadcasting, and each reader wakes the next by calling Thread.Signal(cR) after its LOCK clause in AcquireShared.

front: How is fairness handled for mutexes versus condition variables?
back: For mutexes the thread implementation handles it, typically FIFO within each priority level; mostly the same for condition variables, but sometimes the programmer must get involved. Starvation (a thread never making progress) is the most extreme unfairness.

front: How does writer starvation occur in the readers/writers code under heavy read load?
back: Overlapping readers keep i positive: A acquires (i=1), B acquires (i=2), A releases (i=1), C acquires (i=2), B releases (i=1), and so on. There is always an active reader, i never reaches 0, and writers stay blocked forever.

front: What is the fix for writer starvation in the readers/writers code?
back: Add writeWaiters; AcquireExclusive increments it before its wait loop and decrements after. In AcquireShared, if writeWaiters > 0 a new reader Signals cW and Waits once on cR before its usual loop, so a new reader defers once to a blocked writer.

front: What does Birrell warn about adding scheduling features for fairness?
back: "There is no limit to how complicated this can become"; exercise restraint and add such scheduling features only if the actual load on the resource requires them.

front: How much did the readers/writers solution grow as enhancements were added?
back: From 15 lines in the procedure bodies to 30, with quite subtle correctness reasoning.

front: On what does the decision to handle spurious wake-ups, lock conflicts, and starvation depend?
back: The threads implementation's performance, whether you run on a multiprocessor, and the expected load; if the resource is mostly not in use, adopt the simplest coding style.

front: What is Birrell's rule of thumb about which condition-variable enhancement is worth it?
back: Moving Signal beyond the end of the LOCK clause is usually easy and worth it; the other enhancements usually are not, but ignore them only after explicitly considering whether your situation needs them.

front: How can condition variables deadlock, and what is the remedy?
back: A acquires resource (1), B acquires (2), A waits on (2)'s CV, B waits on (1)'s. Remedy: a partial order on resources managed by condition variables (e.g. (1) before (2)), so B may not acquire (1) while holding (2).

front: Describe the nested monitor problem.
back: Get does LOCK a DO LOCK b DO WHILE NOT ready DO Wait(b,c) END END END; Give does LOCK a DO LOCK b DO ready := TRUE; Signal(c) END END. Get's Wait releases b but keeps a, so Give blocks on a and never signals.

front: When does the nested-monitor deadlock usually arise?
back: When a mutex is locked at one abstraction level and the code calls down into a lower level that (unknown to the higher level) blocks, and the block can be released only by a thread that needs the higher-level mutex. Calling down while holding a mutex is risky unless you know when the callee blocks.

front: What are the fixes for the nested monitor problem, and what reference is cited?
back: Explicitly unlock before calling down (with the earlier dangers), or better, end the LOCK clause before calling down. Reference: Haddon, "Nested monitor calls" [8].

front: What might a straightforward multi-threaded application's threads be doing?
back: One thread for the main computation, one writing output to a file, one waiting for or responding to user input, and one in the background cleaning up data structures (e.g. re-balancing a tree). Several SRC library packages fork threads internally.

front: How should slow devices be driven in a threaded program, and what older schemes become unnecessary?
back: With synchronous library calls that suspend only the calling thread; invoke the device call in a separate thread to avoid waiting, and use multiple threads for multiple outstanding requests. Older asynchronous schemes (interrupts, Unix signals, VMS ASTs) are unnecessary.

front: If the OS still delivers asynchronous events, what should the thread runtime library do?
back: Convert them into more appropriate mechanisms; examples are the Topaz system call design [11] and the exception and trapping machinery of Sun's lightweight process library [14,15].

front: What makes forking UI work require great care?
back: Reading interactive state (current selection, contents of editable text areas) is hazardous because it can change once you run asynchronously; each window system handles this differently and Birrell had "not yet seen a totally satisfactory design."

front: How do window systems differ in how they invoke a program's action, and what must you decide in one case?
back: Some always call the program in a separate thread; others call it synchronously with the input event, in which case you must decide whether to do the action synchronously or fork. Birrell calls it "particularly infuriating" if the display goes dead because a database query is slow.

front: How do RPC servers versus connection-oriented servers use forking?
back: With RPC [3], the server runtime forks threads internally and runs each concurrent incoming call in its own thread, with no work for you. With connection-oriented protocols (e.g. file transfer over TCP), fork one thread per incoming connection.

front: Per Birrell, how does a client avoid waiting for a server reply?
back: It calls the server from a separate thread.

front: What is the simplest variant of deferring work, and its downsides?
back: Once the procedure has computed its result, fork a thread for the rest and return, reducing latency in hope the deferred work is cheaper later. Downsides: possibly large numbers of threads, and the cost of Fork every time.

front: What is the preferred way to defer work instead of forking each time?
back: A single housekeeping thread fed with requests; better still if it needs no information beyond "there is work." It can merge similar requests into one action or run no more often than a chosen periodic interval.

front: On a multiprocessor, what is the one general forking technique Birrell offers?
back: Pipelining; deciding when and what else to fork is too problem-specific for general advice.

front: What is a pipeline, per Birrell?
back: A chain of producer-consumer relationships: A enqueues a request in a buffer, B takes it and does part of the work and enqueues in a second buffer, C does the rest. The three threads run in parallel except when synchronizing on buffers, using up to three processors.

front: What does a pipeline achieve at best, and when is it useful on a uniprocessor?
back: At best almost linear speed-up and full use of a multiprocessor. On a uniprocessor it is useful if each stage hits real-time delays (page faults, device handling, network communication).

front: In the PaintChar/Rasterize/Painter pipeline example, how are the buffers and synchronization implemented?
back: Buffers are unbounded linked lists tracked by tail pointers, initialized to dummy elements; each consumer keeps its own last pointer instead of removing nodes; one mutex m protects both buffers, with condition variables c1 and c2.

front: What is pipelining's second problem (static concurrency)?
back: The number of stages statically determines the amount of concurrency. That is fine if you know the processor count and exactly where real-time delays occur, but a problem in flexible or portable environments.

front: Despite its problems, how does Birrell characterize pipelining?
back: A powerful technique with wide applicability.

front: What must the OS and libraries provide for threads to work well?
back: The OS must not suspend the entire address space when one thread blocks for I/O or a page fault, and the OS and libraries must permit calls from multiple threads in parallel. A well-designed environment exposes facilities as synchronous calls that block only the calling thread.

front: What four performance parameters of a thread implementation should you know?
back: Cost of creating a thread, cost of keeping a blocked thread in existence, cost of a context switch, and cost of a LOCK clause when the mutex is not locked.

front: Why can careless thread addition make a program slower?
back: With significantly more ready threads than processors, performance usually degrades because schedulers are slow at general rescheduling: getting a thread onto an idle processor is fast, but queueing it and later swapping it in for another thread is expensive.

front: Besides scheduling overhead, what other problem do more running threads cause?
back: They are more likely to conflict over mutexes and over resources managed by condition variables.

front: The slowdown warning applies mainly to threads added for what reason, and less for what?
back: Mainly for threads added for performance (parallel actions, deferring work, using multiprocessors); less for threads added for program structure (slow devices, fast mouse response, RPC invocations).

front: Does the slowdown warning apply to blocked threads? How many blocked threads is typical?
back: No, it applies only to ready threads. Blocked threads cost only scheduler data structures and a stack; SRC programs often have many (50 is not uncommon), and there are usually hundreds blocked inside the OS even on personal workstations.

front: How expensive is a Fork even with caching, and what measure of a thread implementation does Birrell suggest?
back: Implementations cache a few terminated thread "carcasses," yet a Fork still costs about two or three re-scheduling decisions, so do not fork too small a computation. A useful measure is the smallest computation for which forking is profitable.

front: From SRC experience on a 5-way multiprocessor, were programmers more likely to create too few or too many threads?
back: They were as likely to err by creating too few threads as too many.

front: Give two examples of good uses of alerts.
back: On a multiprocessor, fork several competing algorithms for the same problem and abort the rest when the first finishes; and abort a long database query when the user clicks CANCEL.
source: Using Alert: diverting the flow of control

front: What is the SRC convention for which procedures should be alertable, and what does "long" mean?
back: Every public-interface procedure that might incur a long computation or long-term wait should be alertable: long computations call TestAlert occasionally and long waits use AlertWait instead of Wait. "Long" means long enough to upset a human user.
source: Using Alert: diverting the flow of control

front: What is the benefit and cost of the alertable-procedure convention?
back: Benefit: the user can always regain control of the application. Cost: callers must be prepared for Alerted to propagate out of these procedures. It is applied less rigorously when an entry point only occasionally causes a long wait.
source: Using Alert: diverting the flow of control

front: What is the second SRC alert convention (who may alert whom)?
back: Alert a thread only if you forked it; e.g. a package must not alert a caller's thread that happens to be executing inside the package. This lets an alert mean "terminate completely."
source: Using Alert: diverting the flow of control

front: Why are alerts, like any asynchronous interrupt mechanism, intrusive?
back: A straightforward flow of control in one thread can be diverted by another thread, which defeats verification by local inspection. Unless used with great restraint they make programs unreadable, unmaintainable, and perhaps incorrect.
source: Using Alert: diverting the flow of control

front: What are the alternatives to alerts when you know where the thread is blocked?
back: If you know which condition variable the thread is blocked on, set a boolean flag and signal that condition variable; a package can offer extra entry points whose purpose is to prod a thread blocked inside it.
source: Using Alert: diverting the flow of control

front: When are alerts most useful?
back: When you do not know exactly where the target is blocked (in any of several packages, or on any of several condition variables); there an alert is the best solution. Even with alternatives, alerts may be preferable as a single unified way to provoke thread termination.
source: Using Alert: diverting the flow of control

front: Was there consensus among thread facility designers on the alert problem?
back: No; there was no consensus, and each solution had its own problems.
source: Using Alert: diverting the flow of control

front: How do abstraction layers carry over to concurrency, and what order do they form?
back: Threads honor abstraction boundaries, and permanent daemon threads inside an abstraction call only lower levels. The layering forms a partial order sufficient to prevent mutex deadlocks with no extra care.

front: When does pure top-down layering fail?
back: When actions affecting high levels originate low: network packet reception, user input, and spontaneous state changes in peripherals such as disks and tapes.

front: Why does strict top-down layering give bad network-receive performance?
back: It costs a context switch per layer, because the thread wanting data from its transport connection cannot be the one dispatching an incoming Ethernet packet (the packet may belong to another connection, protocol, or family). Such implementations had "uniformly bad performance," dominated by context switches.

front: What are up-calls (Clark [5]) and what performance do they give?
back: A pool of threads receives data-link packets; the receiving thread dispatches on protocol type and calls up to the network layer, dispatches again, calls up to transport, and finally to the connection. No unnecessary context switches; all top-performing network implementations are structured this way.

front: What interface cost do up-calls add to each layer?
back: Each layer needs an up-call interface in addition to its down-call interface.

front: Why do up-calls make synchronization more delicate?
back: In a top-down system, holding a layer's mutex while calling down is fine (barring nested-monitor blocking). With up-calls, an up-calling thread holding a lower-level mutex that locks a higher-level one violates the lock order and can deadlock on mutexes alone. Advice: avoid holding a mutex while making an up-call, "easier said than done."

front: What problem do version stamps solve?
back: A lower-level thread may invalidate information a higher-level thread has cached (e.g. a disk volume changes through hardware problems or removal). Up-calls can invalidate higher-level cache structures but not state held locally by a thread: at worst a thread reads from the cache and the data becomes invalid before its call to the lower level happens.

front: Describe the version-stamp technique.
back: The low level keeps a counter with the true data, incremented on every change; every copy handed up carries the current counter value and is cached with it; calls down pass the counter back; the low level compares and, on mismatch, returns an exception (sometimes carrying the new data). Also useful across a distributed system.

front: What does Birrell mean by "an embarrassment of parallelism"?
back: A program can expose far more concurrency than the machine accommodates (e.g. a compiler with a thread per procedure or statement). One thread per action makes the scheduler inefficient, causes numerous lock conflicts, or exhausts memory for stacks.

front: What are work crews (Vandevoorde and Roberts [17])?
back: An abstraction that controls forking: requests for asynchronous activity are enqueued and served by a fixed pool of threads. The complexity lies in managing requests, synchronizing between them, and coordinating results.

front: What is "lazy forking"?
back: An unexplored SRC proposal to implement Fork so it defers actually creating the thread until a processor is available to run it.

front: What four properties must a successful program have, per Birrell's "Building your program"?
back: Useful, correct, live, and efficient; concurrency affects each.

front: For a library to be "useful" to multi-threaded callers, what must be true of all its entry points?
back: They must be thread re-entrant (callable by multiple threads simultaneously), even if each just locks a central mutex.

front: Where must a library designed for multi-threaded callers never return results?
back: In shared global variables or global statically allocated storage.

front: Should a library's calls be synchronous or asynchronous for multi-threaded callers, per Birrell?
back: Synchronous; callers use other threads to get overlap.

front: Should you design library interfaces for multi-threaded callers when there are no multi-threaded clients yet?
back: Yes; Birrell says to follow these rules even without current multi-threaded clients.

front: What does "correct" mean, and what discipline does Birrell demand?
back: If the program produces an answer, it is the one its specification defines. Be fastidious about associating each piece of data with one and only one mutex ("If you don't pay constant attention to this, your task will be hopeless"); with the re-check-after-Wait style you are unlikely to go wrong.

front: What does "live" mean, and what are the alternatives to liveness?
back: The program eventually produces an answer; the alternatives are infinite loops ("I can't help you with infinite loops") or deadlock. Deadlocks should be easy to detect with a symbolic debugger that enumerates threads and shows each stack.

front: What debugger features does Birrell say are desirable for threaded programs?
back: Filtering thread enumeration (threads with a stack frame in a given module, threads blocked on a given mutex or condition variable) and, ideally, finding which thread holds a given mutex.

front: Why are performance bugs the most insidious, and what statistics are needed?
back: You may not notice them. Needed: lock conflicts (how often threads blocked on each mutex and how long they waited) and concurrency levels (average number of ready threads, or percentage of time n threads were ready).

front: What does Birrell say about trading correctness for efficiency?
back: Do not emphasize efficiency at the expense of correctness: it is much easier to make a correct program efficient than an efficient program correct.

front: What does Birrell conclude about the difficulty of concurrent programming, and what do you need?
back: It is neither exotic nor difficult; you need good primitives and suitable libraries, basic caution and carefulness, an armory of useful techniques, and knowledge of the common pitfalls.

front: What does the appendix compare, and what caveats does Birrell give?
back: The SRC design against Apollo, Sun and Mach, with hints on when their differences are useful or dangerous. It assumes familiarity with their documentation; readers should check that documentation first, and Birrell apologizes in advance for any misrepresentation.

front: What mechanisms does the paper skip that every compared design has?
back: Facilities for affecting scheduling (adjusting priorities, hints on when preemption is useful), per-thread context information (SRC and Sun), and a "conditional lock" operation on a mutex (all of them).

front: In what sense are all the compared thread systems equivalent?
back: Equivalent in power: each can reproduce the others' facilities by programming on top of them, and any concurrent problem can be solved with any of them; differences only make some paradigms easier and others harder.

front: In the equivalence table, which SRC facilities does Sun OS 4.0 lack?
back: Join and Alert (Sun has no Join and no Alert).

front: In the equivalence table, which SRC facility does Mach C threads lack, and which does Apollo CPS lack?
back: Mach C threads lack Alert. Apollo Domain CPS has no Signal (its Alert is task_$signal).

front: In Birrell's equivalence table, what are the Sun OS 4.0 equivalents of LOCK/END, Wait, Signal, and Broadcast?
back: LOCK/END = mon_enter/mon_exit (Mutex = mon_t); Wait = cv_wait; Signal = cv_notify; Broadcast = cv_broadcast (Condition = cv_t).

front: What is a legitimate use of Apollo's mutex_$lock timeout, and what caveat does Birrell add?
back: Switch to an alternative algorithm when a mutex is held too long, useful if lock conflicts are common; but you should normally make conflicts rare and short via fine-grained locking, each mutex protecting only the data you intend to touch.

front: Why does Birrell discourage using a mutex timeout to detect or recover from deadlocks?
back: Deadlocks are bugs to be found with a debugger and programmed away.

front: How do Apollo level-2 eventcounts serve the purpose of condition variables?
back: Lock the mutex, inspect data, read the eventcount with ec2_$read, unlock, then ec2_$wait until it is advanced; this matches SRC Wait plus Broadcast.

front: With Apollo eventcounts, what gives the atomicity SRC guarantees in Wait, and how does SRC relate to this?
back: Reading the eventcount (ec2_$read) while still holding the mutex. This is how SRC implements Wait's atomicity.

front: Why is it a drawback that eventcounts are not tied to a mutex or its data?
back: Threads can block and wake without synchronizing over shared data, which is rarely what you want, since you normally wake a thread because you just changed data it cares about.

front: Describe the Apollo eventcount lost-wakeup sequence.
back: (1) A looks at the data and decides to block; (2) A unlocks the mutex; (3) B locks and changes the data; (4) B calls ec2_$advance; (5) A calls ec2_$read; (6) A calls ec2_$wait. A is never woken: step 5 was meant to precede step 4, and to guarantee that, A must do (5) before (2).

front: What is the convenience of ec2_$wait waiting on multiple eventcounts, and its cost?
back: Occasionally convenient; without it you need one thread per awaited condition. It introduces no new problems beyond implementation complexity and possible performance penalties.

front: How does Apollo's task_$signal differ from SRC's alerts, and why does Apollo inhibit faults while a mutex is locked?
back: task_$signal produces a fault at an arbitrary point in the target thread (unless faults are inhibited), unlike SRC's polled alerts. Interrupting a thread holding a mutex would leave shared data unpredictable, so Apollo inhibits faults while a mutex is locked.

front: What is the tradeoff between polled alerts and interrupt-anywhere faults?
back: Polling makes control flow visible in the source; interrupting anywhere outside LOCK clauses makes termination more certain, since forgetting a TestAlert call cannot break it. Both are valid and the ideal design would support both.

front: Why are Sun's "lightweight processes" not true threads?
back: Only one runs at a time within an address space, though creation and synchronization look like real threads.

front: How does Sun handle recursive mutex locking, and what is the danger?
back: Sun allows it (a holder can call a procedure that locks the same mutex); in SRC this deadlocks. It is fine if the monitor invariant was restored before the call, but if the call is really a bug you silently get wrong answers. Splitting the computation across threads can turn it into a deadlock.

front: How does Sun handle alerts, and what does Birrell say about alerts being fundamental?
back: Sun has no alert mechanism, but threads can handle asynchronous Unix signals via agt_create; some signals serve the purpose of alerts. Alerts are "not really a fundamental part of threads," just a convenience.

front: What is Birrell's advice on Sun's message passing between threads?
back: Most designers view message passing as an alternative to shared-memory synchronization, not an adjunct; Birrell advises against using both in one program, except as needed for Sun's message system to handle Unix signals.

front: Where do the table's Mach entries come from, and how does Mach's facility compare to SRC's?
back: From Eric Cooper's C library interface to Mach threads [6]; it closely resembles SRC's, the only noticeable omission is alerting, and there are no substantive differences.

front: On deadlock detection and recovery, how does Birrell's emphasis differ from the notes?
back: The notes list detection and recovery as options; Birrell treats deadlocks as bugs to find with a debugger and remove, and discourages lock timeouts for recovery. It is a difference of emphasis (advice for application programmers), not a factual conflict.

front: On balancing a pipeline, how does the notes' remedy differ from Birrell's?
back: The notes assign more pool threads to the slow stage; Birrell's pipeline has one thread per stage, balanced by hand-tuning how much work each stage does, and he notes the stage count statically fixes concurrency. Both are standard remedies, not a contradiction.
